nameStory: This little plant gets its name from its leaves, which are shaped remarkably like tiny ivy leaves with their lobed edges. The 'speedwell' part comes from an old English farewell blessing - 'speed well' meant 'travel safely' - perhaps because these small flowers were thought to bring good fortune to travelers who noticed them along their path.
description: Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell is a tiny, low-growing annual plant that you might easily overlook if you're not looking carefully. This delicate European native has naturalized in parts of New England, forming small patches of ivy-shaped leaves close to the ground. The plant rarely grows more than a few inches tall, with small pinkish flowers that appear almost too dainty for the outdoors.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, rounded leaves with 3-5 shallow lobes that look remarkably like miniature ivy leaves. They feel soft and slightly fuzzy to the touch, with a fresh, mild green scent when crushed.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny pink to pale blue flowers, each only about 1/8 inch across with four petals. The flowers are so small you might need to get down close to really appreciate their delicate beauty.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, rarely rising more than 2-4 inches high. The stems are slender and somewhat trailing, creating small patches.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, heart-shaped seed capsules that split open when mature. The seeds are tiny and easily scattered by wind or foot traffic.

habitat: Look for Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell in disturbed soils, along path edges, in gardens, and other areas where the ground has been worked or compacted. It prefers somewhat sandy or loamy soils and can tolerate partial shade, often appearing in spots where few other plants can establish.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge early and begin flowering, with the tiny pink blooms appearing as soon as the weather warms. This is the best time to spot the fresh, bright green foliage.
seasonality.summer: Continues flowering through early summer, though plants may struggle in very hot, dry conditions. Seeds begin forming and dispersing.
seasonality.fall: Plants typically complete their life cycle and die back, leaving seeds to overwinter in the soil for next year's growth.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts visible - this annual plant survives only as seeds waiting in the soil for spring warmth to trigger germination.

funFact: Despite being incredibly tiny and easily overlooked, this little speedwell is actually quite the world traveler - it managed to cross the Atlantic Ocean and establish itself in North America, proving that sometimes the smallest adventurers are the most successful!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with its close relative, regular Ivy-leaved Speedwell, which has blue flowers instead of pink ones. Remember: pink flowers mean 'pink ivy-leaved,' blue flowers mean regular ivy-leaved speedwell.
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes called 'false ivy-leaved speedwell' in scientific contexts, which can be confusing since there's also a 'true' ivy-leaved speedwell. The main difference is flower color - this pink-flowered species is the 'false' one, while the blue-flowered version is considered the 'true' ivy-leaved speedwell.
compareHints: Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves. The combination of pink flowers and lobed leaves makes it quite distinctive once you know what to look for, though you'll need sharp eyes to spot this tiny plant.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
